catalog_quote: Stress in Maropa has been described as to be placed on the penultimate syllable of a lexical item (Cf. GUILLAUME, 2012). It is true that in most roots the stress-bearing unit is placed in the penultimate syllable of a phonological word like the examples in (2); however, some elements display different stress and pitch patterns depending on some morphophonological processes or syntactic relations. ... When some suffixes and enclitics are attached to content words, primary stress may move one syllable to the right, depending on the number of morphemes added to the roots, and the number of syllables of these bound forms as in (5). ... [p.16] the enclitics =´in ‘INTNS’ and =´jj ‘AUG’ attract the primary stress to the last syllable of the phonological word to which they attach. ... audit.reasoning: Quote check: every fragment of the deciding quotation, the heavy-syllable quote, the exceptions quote and the domain quote are verbatim in the held publisher PDF of Gallinate 2020 at the stated sections/pages. Deciding source: a 2020 fieldwork-based phonology article with pitch measurements, the only dedicated treatment of Maropa prosody; Glottolog has 2 descriptive refs total, neither a fuller stress source. Guillaume's 2024 Takanan handbook chapter (fetched sources now from HAL) confirms the penult default and explicitly says his own 2012 statement was not based on detailed investigation and the system is likely more complex, which is consistent with our hedged coding (penult default over the PWd; final CVC created by two enclitics attracts stress; author's own culminativity/M-H-L residue flagged). sources.quote: 'For Reyesano, I have argued that stress falls on the penultimate syllable and shown evidence for this in a certain number of words (Guillaume 2012a: 199). However, this conclusion was not based on detailed investigation and the system is likely to be more complex.' Also: Takanan accentual systems 'delimit the phonological/prosodic word; none of them are lexically/morphologically contrastive'.
